name: Optical Brighteners
title: Optical Brighteners in Laundry Detergent: Safe or Not? — IngredientIQ
description: Optical brighteners make whites look whiter by clinging to fabric and reflecting UV light. They stay on clothes against your skin and don't biodegrade well. Who should skip them.
subtitle: The reason your whites 'glow' in sunlight. They don't clean anything — they coat fabric with a fluorescent dye that stays there.
quickAnswer: Optical brighteners (also called fluorescent whitening agents) are dyes that absorb ultraviolet light and re-emit it as visible blue, making fabric look whiter and brighter. They work by staying on the cloth after washing, which means they're in constant contact with skin. They're a minor contact allergen, they can cause photosensitivity in a few people, and most are poorly biodegradable and toxic to aquatic life. Not dangerous for most people; worth avoiding for babies, eczema, and anyone who wants their laundry actually clean rather than optically clean.
foundInShort: Laundry detergent, fabric softener, some paper and cosmetics
whatItIs: Optical brighteners are synthetic dyes — most based on stilbene, coumarin, or biphenyl structures — that fluoresce. They absorb invisible UV light and emit it as blue visible light, which cancels the yellowish tinge that white fabric develops with age and washing.
They're designed to bind to cotton and other fibres and resist rinsing. Every wash tops up the coating. Under a blacklight, brightener-treated clothing glows; that's the dye you're wearing.
whatItDoes: Nothing in the way of cleaning. Brighteners don't remove stains or dirt; they mask the dull appearance of fabric so it looks cleaner than it is. Detergent makers include them because consumers judge cleaning by whiteness.
They're also in some paper, plastics, and cosmetics for the same reason, and in 'brightening' laundry boosters.
safety: Acute toxicity is low, and skin absorption of the common brighteners is minimal. The concerns are modest and chronic. Because the dye stays on fabric, skin — especially a baby's, or eczema-prone skin — is in continuous contact with it. Allergic contact dermatitis to optical brighteners is documented but uncommon; it's more often found in people already reacting to fragrances or other laundry residues.
Some brighteners are photosensitisers: under UV light they can generate reactive species on the skin. Reports of photoallergic reactions exist but are rare.

The more consistent problem is environmental. Stilbene brighteners are poorly biodegradable, are toxic to fish and aquatic invertebrates, and are among the most frequently detected synthetic compounds in surface water downstream of wastewater plants. The EU Ecolabel and several eco-certification schemes exclude them for this reason.
They are not carcinogenic by current assessments and are not restricted for health reasons in any major jurisdiction.
whoShouldAvoid: Babies and young children — brightener-free 'baby' detergents exist for this reason
Anyone with eczema, sensitive skin, or unexplained rashes in areas covered by clothing (waistband, underarm, collar)
People with photosensitivity conditions or on photosensitising medication
Households on septic systems or in areas with sensitive waterways
Anyone who wants to see when clothes are actually clean — brighteners hide the difference

regulatory.status: Permitted in detergents; excluded from EU Ecolabel and Nordic Swan certified products on environmental grounds. Some individual brighteners are registered under REACH with aquatic-toxicity classifications.
Permitted; no restriction. Excluded from EPA Safer Choice certified products.

commonProducts: Most mainstream laundry detergents (powder and liquid)
Some fabric softeners and dryer sheets
A few skin-brightening cosmetics and some sunscreens
alternatives: Detergents labelled 'no optical brighteners' or 'free & clear'
Oxygen bleach (sodium percarbonate) for actual whitening
Bluing agents — an older trick that washes out
Line-drying whites in sunlight, which does bleach them

faqs.a: Not in a meaningful way for humans at laundry exposures. The health concerns are allergy and photosensitivity in a small number of people. The stronger case against them is environmental persistence and aquatic toxicity.

faqs.q: Why do my clothes glow under a blacklight?
faqs.a: Because optical brighteners from your detergent are coating them. That's what they're designed to do — and why hunters and some outdoor users avoid brightener-treated clothing, since animals can see the UV glow.
No. They make fabric reflect more light so it appears whiter. Dirt and residue are still there. Detergents without brighteners may look less impressive on whites but clean just as well.

faqs.q: Can I remove optical brighteners from clothes?
faqs.a: Partially, over many washes with a brightener-free detergent. Some outdoor retailers sell strippers for this purpose, mainly for hunting clothing.

related.label: Sodium lauryl sulfate — in many detergents
